Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization
Xinzhuang Xiong, Yonghao Wang, Shengyao Sun, Chengxi Li, and Evangeline Young
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, The Chinese University of Hong Kong
Abstract—Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using
EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand-
engineered. We present Meta-RTL, an EDA-grounded framework that
evolves RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop while keeping the
optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared
with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL∗reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by
7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70%
of them. Without further evolution, Meta-RTL∗transfers to 10 unseen
IC-RTL designs, reducing aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0%
and total synthesized area by 12.6%. We further characterize three search
mechanisms in the evolved harness and assess their contributions through
ablations and a case study.
I. INTRODUCTION
Optimizing register-transfer-level (RTL) designs for timing and area
is a critical task in digital hardware design. Functionally equivalent
RTL descriptions can synthesize into substantially different circuits,
so the way a design is written directly determines its timing and
area. Synthesis tools [1], [2] apply predefined optimization passes and
heuristics, but they optimize within the structure that the RTL expresses
rather than changing it. Designers therefore restructure RTL manually,
with each revision followed by functional verification, synthesis, and
timing–area analysis. This iterative process is labor-intensive and
difficult to scale as designs grow more complex.
Large language models (LLMs) have opened new opportunities
to automate this process. Early studies generated RTL from high-
level specifications, improving generation quality through domain-
specific fine-tuning and functional validation [3]–[5]. Later approaches
fed compilation, simulation, and PPA results back to the model to
iteratively refine generated designs [6], [7]. Recent agentic frameworks
go further, coupling LLM reasoning with EDA tools to generate, verify,
and optimize RTL designs autonomously [8]–[13].
For such agents, how the search is organized matters as much
as which transformations the LLM proposes. Every candidate must
remain functionally equivalent, timing and area often conflict, and
each evaluation requires synthesis and equivalence checking. The
search is governed by the agent’s harness: the executable procedure
that presents EDA feedback to the model, decides which candidates
to keep, and allocates the evaluation budget. It therefore shapes both
optimization quality and cost [14]. Existing agents differ precisely
in these choices, from predefined workflows for tool invocation and
iterative rewriting [9]–[11] to persistent memory, reusable skills, and
shared candidate pools [12], [13], [15]. Yet all of these harnesses
are designed by hand, and each embeds fixed assumptions about
how optimization should proceed. Promoting only the best-scoring
candidate, for example, assumes that good designs are reached through
steady improvement, whereas profitable restructuring often passes
through intermediate designs that look worse before they are refined.
In these agents, EDA feedback improves the designs but not the
harness that produces them.
This raises a natural question: Without manually prescribing sophis-
ticated search heuristics, can we evolve RTL optimization harnesses
from EDA feedback that outperform hand-designed ones—and if so,
what makes the evolved harnesses effective?
Fig. 1 Meta-RTL∗versus Dr. RTL on 20 development and 10 unseen
designs. Triplets show relative reductions in WNS/TNS violations and
area; blue/orange indicates improvement/regression.
To answer these questions, we present Meta-RTL, which evolves
an RTL optimization harness from a minimal seed through two nested
loops. In the inner loop, a fixed LLM optimizes RTL designs under
the current harness. In the outer loop, a proposer LLM improves the
harness much as an engineer would: it traces EDA failures in the
inner-loop logs back to specific harness decisions, hypothesizes a
targeted fix and its expected effect, probes the fix on a few relevant
designs, and revises it based on the evidence. Each submitted harness
is then frozen and scored on all development designs by synthesis and
equivalence checking outside its control. In this way, EDA feedback
improves not only the designs but also the harness that produces
them. While skill libraries capture what transformations to apply,
Meta-RTL learns how to search for effective transformations, turning
a traditionally hand-designed process into an optimization target.
The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:
• We formulate EDA-grounded harness evolution for RTL timing–
area optimization, in which the search procedure itself evolves
from a minimal loop under a fixed LLM, EDA flow, and budget
per design. Its proposer revises harnesses through four designed
stages described in Section III-C.
• We show that harness evolution yields substantial timing and
area gains (Fig. 1). Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL∗reduces
aggregate WNS/TNS violation magnitudes by 7.8%/11.0% and
area on 14 of 20 development designs (Section IV-B). Without
further evolution, it also improves WNS, TNS, and area on 7, 8,
and 7 of the 10 unseen designs, respectively (Section IV-C).
• We identify three search mechanisms that emerge in the evolved
harness, and further assess their contributions through targeted
ablations and a circuit-level case study (Sections IV-E and IV-F).

II. RELATED WORK
A. Conventional Synthesis and RTL Optimization
Traditional hardware optimization relies on logic synthesis and
physical design tools to improve area and timing. Early synthesis
systems such as SIS [16] introduced systematic logic and sequential
circuit optimization. Yosys [1] provides an extensible framework for
RTL synthesis, while ABC [2] supports AIG-based logic optimization
and technology mapping. OpenROAD [17] enables automated physical
design through placement, routing, and timing optimization. These
tools employ well-established optimization algorithms, but high-level
RTL restructuring still relies on manual design expertise.
B. LLM-Based RTL Optimization
Recent studies leverage LLMs for iterative RTL optimization, in
which candidate designs are repeatedly rewritten and evaluated with
EDA feedback [10], [11], [18]. Dr. RTL [12] introduces reusable
optimization skills distilled from tool feedback. RTLScout [13] instead
exploits shared candidate pools and experience accumulated across
runs. Despite these advances, the executable procedures organizing
optimization remain largely hand-engineered.
Building on broader progress in self-evolving systems [19]–[21],
recent studies have explored program evolution for EDA tasks. These
include logic synthesis [22], technology mapping [23], and physical
design tasks such as placement [24], [25], routing [26], and FPGA
place-and-route [27]. Similar approaches have also been applied to
hardware design [28] and verification [29].
Unlike approaches that evolve internal EDA heuristics, Meta-RTL
evolves the executable search procedure of RTL optimization agents.
We investigate whether synthesis and equivalence-checking feedback
can guide this evolution to outperform hand-engineered agents and
generalize to unseen designs.
III. META-RTL
A. Overview
As shown in Fig. 2, Meta-RTL evolves executable RTL optimization
harnesses from a minimal loop H0 that simply edits RTL and evaluates
the resulting designs using default EDA reports. An agentic proposer
P progressively revises the harness using the implementations and
execution evidence of earlier rounds, and the evaluation protocol
specifies how it interacts with the fixed evaluator.
For an RTL design D and resource budget B, a harness H(D, B)
defines an inner optimization procedure that coordinates a fixed
LLM M with equivalence checking, synthesis, and timing analysis.
Its execution produces a trajectory τ containing RTL candidates,
tool outcomes, timing–area measurements, and search decisions. The
harness determines how candidates are constructed, how feedback is
presented, and how subsequent transformations are explored.
An archive A stores harness implementations, evaluation results,
and execution trajectories. Harnesses are ranked by normalized timing–
area utility Q(H) (Section III-D), and the highest-scoring eligible
harness, Meta-RTL∗, is selected and then evaluated on unseen designs.
B. Harness Representation and Search Space
A harness H is a self-contained Python package that orchestrates
the inner optimization loop via two primitives: invoking the fixed LLM
M and querying the fixed EDA evaluator for synthesis, timing, and
sequential equivalence checking (SEC). H can freely define prompt
templates, helper scripts, and search routines, through which evolution
may modify four aspects of the search procedure: (1) candidate
construction, (2) feedback organization, (3) search-state management,
and (4) resource allocation and search control.
Harnesses execute in Bubblewrap-isolated environments. The in-
dependent evaluator, which cannot be accessed or modified by the
2


--- Page 3 ---
proposer P or H, fixes the optimization LLM, EDA flow, synthesis
constraints, equivalence checking, scoring objective, and per-design
budgets. This isolation ensures a consistent and reliable evaluation
protocol while allowing the executable search procedure to evolve.
Consequently, neither P nor H can relax verification constraints or
alter scoring logic, so all gains can be attributed to improved search.
C. Evidence-Guided Harness Evolution
The proposer P is an LLM agent that can read the archive A, edit
harness code, and launch probe runs. At each round, it selects as
parent Hpar the harness it judges most promising, which need not be
the highest-scoring one, based on the implementations, scores, and
run records of all archived harnesses. This lets evolution continue
from a harness whose new mechanism looks promising in its traces
before it pays off in score. Its instructions then prescribe four stages,
shown at the bottom of Fig. 2, for developing revisions from Hpar
and its run records Tpar.
EDA Failure Attribution. The proposer inspects Tpar, including
RTL edits, SEC diagnostics, WNS/TNS/area trajectories, and resource
usage, to trace how candidate transformations fare in correctness
checking and EDA evaluation. It identifies recurring failures and
unproductive search behavior, and attributes them to the responsible
harness decisions, such as how candidates are constructed or how
search state is managed. A score alone cannot provide this information:
a harness whose edits fail SEC and one whose valid edits bring no
gain may both score zero. The resulting diagnosis names a bottleneck
together with the traces that support it.
Harness Hypothesis Generation. The proposer turns the diagnosis
into a hypothesis: a targeted change to relevant code paths, prompts,
or tool interfaces, paired with a testable prediction of how search
behavior should change. Typical predictions include more candidates
passing SEC, broader exploration, or fewer unproductive evaluations.
Stating the prediction in advance makes a probe informative even
when the score barely moves, and keeps a lucky gain from being
credited to the change. The proposer then implements it, and the
prediction decides which designs to probe and how to read the results.
Cost-Aware Probing. The proposer runs the revised harness on
development designs selected for their relevance to the bottleneck, their
ability to test the prediction, and their evaluation cost. Because Hpar
has already run on the same designs, comparing the new traces with
Tpar isolates the effect of the change and shows whether the predicted
behavior occurred, for example in candidate validity, optimization
progress, or resource usage. Each candidate is limited to K probe
runs. Since a full-set evaluation runs every development design under
budget B, these probes give an early signal at a fraction of its cost.
Evidence-Based Revision. The proposer uses the probe results to
accept, refine, or replace the hypothesis. Confirmed improvements are
developed further, while failed predictions and regressions lead to a
revised implementation or a new hypothesis. Failed predictions are
also informative, since they rule out a suspected cause and sharpen the
next diagnosis. The proposer may cycle through hypothesis generation,
probing, and revision within the K-run limit, but each candidate must
end in a submitted harness.
Each round produces up to C candidate harnesses. Every submitted
harness is frozen and formally evaluated on the full development
set Ddev under budget B to obtain Q(H), and only harnesses that
complete this evaluation are eligible for selection. The archive records
every harness together with its lineage, score, and run records, so
later rounds build on all accumulated evidence. After R rounds, the
eligible harness with the highest Q(H) is selected as Meta-RTL∗.
D. EDA-Grounded Harness Evaluation
Harness evaluation measures the RTL quality that a complete
optimization run achieves under fixed resource and EDA constraints.
Each run starts from the original design D. The returned RTL ˜D is
eligible for scoring only if it passes correctness checking and yields
valid synthesis measurements. The original design remains available
as a fallback with zero normalized utility.
Normalized Timing–Area Utility. Meta-RTL uses an equivalent
formulation of the timing–area score in Dr. RTL [12]. For a completed
run τ(H, D, B), the normalized gain in each metric m is defined as
gm(τ) = m(D) −m( ˜D)

where WNS, TNS, and A denote worst negative slack, total negative
slack, and area, respectively. Run utility is defined as
q(τ) = αgWNS(τ) + βgTNS(τ) + γgA(τ)
−λ1[A( ˜D) > (1 + ρ)A(D)].
(2)
α, β, and γ weight the normalized gains, while λ penalizes relative
area growth exceeding ρ. Larger utility indicates greater timing–area
optimization gains relative to the original design.
Harness quality is the mean development-set utility:

Normalization measures improvement relative to each original design,
while averaging summarizes performance across the development set.
All methods use the same scoring parameters (Section IV-A).
Resource-Constrained Execution. Each inner optimization run
receives a budget B = (BEDA, BLLM), enforcing
nEDA ≤BEDA,
cLLM ≤BLLM,
(4)
where nEDA counts candidate EDA evaluations and cLLM denotes
cumulative LLM API cost, accounting for cached inputs, uncached
inputs, and output tokens. The shared evaluator enforces both limits
independently of harness decisions.
IV. EXPERIMENTS
A. Experimental Setup
We compare Meta-RTL∗with two strong LLM-based RTL opti-
mization frameworks: Dr. RTL [12] with its released skill library and
RTLScout [13]. For RTLScout, we only evaluate its RTL optimization
component while keeping the synthesis flow fixed.
Evaluation Benchmarks. Our experiments use two benchmark
suites, Dr. RTL [12] and IC-RTL [11]. The Dr. RTL benchmark
contains 20 designs covering arithmetic, control, communication, and
sequential logic, which serve as the development set. IC-RTL contains
10 more complex designs spanning image processing, compression,
geometric computation, and hardware acceleration. These designs are
held out from harness evolution to evaluate generalization.
Outer Evolution. Evolution begins with a minimal seed: an in-place
RTL editing loop guided by default EDA reports. GPT-5.6 Sol [30]
serves as the harness proposer, generating up to C = 2 candidates per
round. We conduct R = 8 evolution rounds, yielding 16 submitted
harnesses in total. Each candidate is limited to K = 5 probe runs on
proposer-selected designs. Submitted harnesses are evaluated afresh
on all 20 development designs under the fixed inner budget. The
highest-scoring eligible harness is selected as Meta-RTL∗.
Inner Optimization. All methods share the same EDA flow and
use DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash [31] as the optimization model. Synopsys

Design Compiler [32] is used for synthesis and timing analysis, and
Cadence JasperGold [33] for SEC. To assess RTL-level improvements
beyond standard synthesis optimizations, we synthesize with a
commercial tool and the Nangate 45 nm [34] standard-cell library.
Following Dr. RTL [12], we impose a stringent 0.1 ns clock period to
drive aggressive timing optimization. All methods share per-design
budgets of BEDA = 50 EDA evaluations and BLLM ≈US$6 in LLM
API cost. The 50-evaluation cap matches Dr. RTL’s 10 major rounds
of five minor attempts each.
Evaluation Metrics. We report worst negative slack (WNS), total
negative slack (TNS), synthesized area (A), and normalized timing–
area utility (Q). The utility metric, defined in Section III-D, uses
(α, β, γ) = (0.50, 0.35, 0.15), λ = 0.50, and ρ = 0.10, following
Dr. RTL [12]. Higher utility indicates better timing–area optimization.
Computational Cost. Under DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash pricing, the
estimated costs of optimizing all 20 development designs are US$22.5
for Meta-RTL∗, US$75 for Dr. RTL, and US$12 for RTLScout.
The total recorded LLM API expenditure was US$627.09, excluding
infrastructure costs (e.g., EDA licenses).
The C × R = 16 candidate harnesses yield an estimated evolution
cost of US$510 (16×US$22.5, i.e., Meta-RTL∗’s cost per candidate,
plus US$150 for GPT-5.6 Sol proposals). Amortizing this cost over
later applications, Meta-RTL∗would become more cost-efficient than
Dr. RTL after about 200 design optimizations, even ignoring the effort
behind the hand-engineered baselines.
B. Development-Set Performance
Table I compares Meta-RTL∗with Dr. RTL and RTLScout on the 20
development designs. Among the three methods, Meta-RTL∗achieves
the best or tied-best WNS on 18 designs, the best TNS on 14 designs,
and the lowest area on 8 designs.
The results show a strong advantage in timing. Compared with
RTLScout, Meta-RTL∗achieves better WNS on 19 designs, ties on
one, and improves TNS on 17 designs, while RTLScout obtains lower
area on 12 designs. Timing gains also coincide with area reductions:
compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL∗improves or maintains both WNS
and TNS while reducing area on 10 designs, including 7 designs with
strict improvements in all three metrics.

Overall, Meta-RTL∗achieves the highest mean normalized utility of
0.2630, compared with 0.1866 for Dr. RTL and 0.1511 for RTLScout,
indicating the strongest aggregate timing–area performance.
C. Generalization to Unseen Designs
To evaluate generalization, we compare Meta-RTL∗with Dr. RTL
on 10 unseen IC-RTL designs. Both methods leverage optimization
experience from the 20-design Dr. RTL benchmark: Dr. RTL through
its distilled skill library, and Meta-RTL through harness evolution. For
a fair comparison, we exclude RTLScout from the transfer evaluation,
as it was not developed on the same benchmark. The skill library and
evolved harness are kept fixed during evaluation on IC-RTL.
Table II presents the timing and area results. Meta-RTL∗achieves
better WNS on 7 designs, better TNS on 8, and lower area on 7. It
also achieves higher utility on 8 of the 10 designs. Notably, on REF,
Meta-RTL∗simultaneously improves WNS, TNS, and area by 45.7%,
26.7%, and 25.6%, respectively. Overall, its mean utility reaches
0.2660, compared with 0.1388 for Dr. RTL, representing a 91.6%
relative improvement. Note that REF contributes substantially to the
aggregate timing gains, yet Meta-RTL∗still achieves 79.0% higher
mean utility on the remaining nine designs. These results indicate that
the evolved harness transfers effectively to unseen designs.

--- Page 5 ---
Fig. 3 Evolution lineage of Meta-RTL harnesses.
D. Evolution Analysis
Evolutionary Progress. Fig. 3 traces the evolution of Meta-RTL∗.
Starting from the minimal loop, Local Feedback extracts critical-path
information and achieves a utility of 0.0936. Serial Dual Context then
improves utility to 0.1265 by revisiting timing-improved candidates
for area recovery.
The subsequent evolution exemplifies how the proposer translates
execution evidence into harness revisions. Inspecting Serial Dual
Context trajectories, the proposer identified repeated RTL editing
failures and premature search termination that prevented structural
transformations from reaching EDA evaluation. It diagnosed a delivery/
continuation bottleneck and hypothesized that programmatic RTL
transformations and bounded search continuation would enable more
valid measurements. Targeted probing on four development designs
increased mean utility from 0.0817 to 0.2263, with previously un-
successful transformations passing SEC. The resulting Programmatic
Relay achieved a full-set utility of 0.2332.
Further evolution revealed the overhead of repeatedly regenerating
transformation programs, motivating persistent artifacts and incremen-
tal program edits. Although Adaptive Workbench temporarily dipped
to 0.2060 due to unpruned workspace state across retries, selecting
it as the parent allowed the proposer to isolate this bottleneck and
introduce structured artifact indexing, yielding Artifact Workbench
(Q = 0.2630, selected as Meta-RTL∗).
Discovered Mechanisms. The lineage reveals three complementary
search mechanisms in Meta-RTL∗.
EDA-Grounded Transformation Guidance. The evolved harness links
EDA feedback to targeted structural transformations. By interpreting
critical-path evidence and timing–area measurements, it guides the
LLM toward transformations such as arithmetic sharing, control
simplification, and common-logic factoring. Subsequent EDA results
then refine the diagnosis, closing an evidence-guided loop.
Executable Transformation Workspace. The evolved harness main-
tains executable transformation programs with their intermediate
artifacts and execution feedback across model requests. Rather than
regenerating RTL edits from scratch, the optimizer can inspect, revise,

and rerun them. This enables incremental construction and debugging
of complex structural rewrites, including repairs of failed attempts.
Pareto Frontier Memory. The evolved harness retains verified RTL
candidates representing different trade-offs among WNS, TNS, and
area. Rather than committing to a single incumbent, the optimizer
can revisit promising intermediate candidates and explore alternative
optimization directions. This preserves opportunities for further timing
or area improvements that might otherwise be lost during the search.
E. Ablation Studies
Effect of Harness Evolution. To assess the benefit of harness
evolution, we compare Meta-RTL with direct harness design. Using
the same proposer, 16 harnesses are independently developed from the
same minimal seed, each with up to K = 5 probe runs but no access
to other candidates or their execution histories. All are evaluated under
the same protocol, and the best is further tested on unseen designs.
Fig. 4 shows the utility of the 16 independently designed harnesses.
The best achieves 0.1813, below both Dr. RTL (0.1866) and Meta-
RTL∗(0.2630). Their mean utility is 0.1376. On unseen designs,
the selected harness achieves 0.1050, compared with 0.2660 for
Meta-RTL∗. These results highlight the benefit of accumulating and
organizing execution evidence across harness revisions.
Contributions of Evolved Mechanisms. To assess the contributions
of the three discovered mechanisms, we construct three ablated variants
of Meta-RTL∗by individually disabling EDA-grounded transformation
guidance (−Guidance), Pareto frontier memory (−Frontier), and the
executable transformation workspace (−Workspace). All variants are
evaluated on the same 10 unseen IC-RTL designs under identical
LLM, EDA flow, and budgets, with other components unchanged.
Table III reports the normalized timing–area utility. Removing
Guidance, Frontier, and Workspace reduces the mean utility from

0.2660 to 0.2064, 0.1889, and 0.1707, respectively, corresponding to
decreases of 22.4%, 29.0%, and 35.8%. The full harness outperforms
these variants on 8, 9, and 10 of the 10 designs, respectively.
Workspace removal causes the largest degradation, with lower utility
on every unseen design. On REF, removing Workspace or Frontier
reduces utility from 0.484 to 0.122 or 0.130, respectively. Removing
Workspace also lowers utility on CONV from 0.131 to 0.027. These
results demonstrate the complementary roles of retaining executable
transformations for iterative refinement and preserving promising RTL
candidates for continued exploration.
F. A Case Study
Fig. 5 illustrates, on the controller design, how the discovered
mechanisms interact within the final Meta-RTL∗harness.
Dr. RTL employs repeated five-way candidate expansion and single-
candidate promotion, but its search remains focused on expanded
decoding without exploring alternative structural directions. Despite
evaluating 50 subsequent candidates, it fails to overcome the area
penalty, leaving the original v0 as the best design. RTLScout carries
the best design from each run into subsequent runs, but abandons the
promising one-hot encoding in v14, ultimately settling for a suboptimal
four-bit encoding without further refinement.
Through harness evolution, Meta-RTL∗gains the ability to identify,
preserve, and revisit promising intermediate designs. The evolved
harness maintains a Pareto frontier of designs, restores their RTL
sources across optimization contexts, and exposes executable interfaces
for reusing saved transformation programs. These mechanisms make
intermediate designs reusable starting points for structural refinement,
even when their immediate optimization scores worsen.
Here, v6 uses a two-bit group/two-bit index encoding to reduce
worst-path logic depth from eight to five levels, but retains per-state
output decoding with a 14.2% area overhead. The harness preserves v6
in frontier memory, excludes the dominated v7–v10, and later restores
v6 to apply the saved program w51. By exploiting the common two-
bit prefix of four states asserting bypass_rk, w51 replaces their
decoding branches with one predicate, reducing the fan-in cone from 23
to 2 cells and total combinational cells from 247 to 188. The resulting
v11 passes equivalence checking and reduces area and WNS/TNS
violations by 8.2%, 18.4%, and 16.1%, respectively, relative to v0,
Dr. RTL’s best result. It also matches RTLScout’s best WNS with 7.0%
lower area. As a structural stepping stone, v11 provides factored output
logic that subsequent candidates reuse and refine through further state
recoding, ultimately yielding v22 (Table I).
V. LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
Our results establish the feasibility and effectiveness of EDA-
grounded harness evolution under a fixed proposer model, optimization
model, EDA flow, and technology library. However, given the
computational budget, the robustness of these findings to LLM
stochasticity warrants further evaluation through repeated trials.
Future work could investigate how different proposer and optimiza-
tion models shape the search strategies discovered through evolution.
Evaluating across technology libraries and physical design flows would
further examine the transferability of these strategies under different
hardware constraints. Beyond RTL optimization, extending harness
evolution to other EDA tasks may reveal new mechanisms arising
from distinct feedback signals and search spaces.
VI. CONCLUSION
We presented Meta-RTL, which evolves executable RTL optimiza-
tion harnesses under a fixed LLM and EDA flow. Compared with
Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL∗reduces aggregate WNS and TNS violations by
7.8% and 11.0% on 20 development designs and transfers without
further evolution to 10 unseen designs, where it nearly doubles
mean utility (0.2660 vs. 0.1388). Analysis and ablations identify
EDA-grounded transformation guidance, an executable transformation
workspace, and a Pareto frontier memory as key mechanisms. These
findings show that EDA feedback can improve not only RTL designs,
but also the search procedures used to optimize them.
